content: The evidence supporting patient-delivered therapy (PDT) is derived from three clinical trials involving heterosexual men and women diagnosed with chlamydia or gonorrhea. Despite these variations, PDT, which involves providing medications or prescriptions directly to patients for their partners, has been shown to prevent reinfection of the index case and is associated with a higher likelihood of partner notification compared to unassisted patient referral of partners. Medications and prescriptions provided for PDT should always be accompanied by clear treatment instructions, appropriate warnings about medication use during pregnancy, general health counseling, and advice for partners to seek personal medical evaluations, especially women presenting with symptoms of STDs or pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Current data suggest that expedited partner therapy (EPT) has limited utility in managing trichomoniasis and is not supported for routine syphilis management. Additionally, there is no experience with EPT for gonorrhea or chlamydia infections among men who have sex with men (MSM). Operational barriers, including unclear legal status in some states, make EPT infeasible in many settings. Accurate and timely reporting of STDs is critical for monitoring morbidity trends, allocating resources effectively, and assisting local health authorities in partner notification and treatment efforts. STD/HIV and AIDS cases must be reported in accordance with state and local statutory requirements. Diseases such as syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, chancroid, HIV infection, and AIDS are reportable in every state, while reporting requirements for other STDs vary by state. Clinicians should familiarize themselves with these requirements and seek guidance from state or local health departments or STD programs if uncertain. STD and HIV reports are strictly confidential and, in most jurisdictions, are protected by statute from subpoena. Before public health representatives follow up on a positive STD test result, they should consult the patient’s healthcare provider to confirm the diagnosis and treatment. Intrauterine or perinatally transmitted STDs can have severe consequences for pregnant women, their partners, and their fetuses. All pregnant women and their sexual partners should be screened for STDs, counseled about the risks of perinatal infections, and provided access to treatment if necessary. Recommended Screening Tests for Pregnant Women: 1. HIV Testing: All pregnant women in the United States should be tested for HIV as early as possible during pregnancy. Testing should be conducted after notifying the woman that it is part of routine prenatal tests unless she declines (opt-out screening). Women who decline testing should have their concerns addressed, and providers should continue to encourage testing. Women with a prior negative HIV test should be informed of the importance of retesting during each pregnancy. Retesting in the third trimester, preferably before 36 weeks of gestation, is recommended for women at high risk of acquiring HIV (e.g., those with STDs during pregnancy, multiple sexual partners, or HIV-infected partners). Rapid HIV testing should be performed on women in labor with undocumented HIV status. If a rapid test is positive, antiretroviral prophylaxis (with consent) should be initiated without waiting for confirmatory test results. 2. Syphilis Testing: A serologic test for syphilis should be performed on all pregnant women at the first prenatal visit. In populations with suboptimal prenatal care, rapid plasma reagin (RPR) card test screening and treatment, if reactive, should be conducted when pregnancy is confirmed. Women at high risk for syphilis, those living in areas with high syphilis morbidity, or those with positive serology in the first trimester should be screened again early in the third trimester (28 weeks of gestation) and at delivery. Some states mandate syphilis screening at delivery. Infants should not be discharged from the hospital unless the mother’s syphilis serologic status has been determined at least once during pregnancy and preferably again at delivery. Any woman delivering a stillborn infant should be tested for syphilis. 3. Hepatitis B Testing: All pregnant women should be routinely tested for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) during an early prenatal visit (first trimester) in each pregnancy, regardless of prior vaccination or testing. Women not screened prenatally, those engaging in high-risk behaviors (e.g., multiple sexual partners, recent STD treatment, injecting drug use, or HBsAg-positive partners), and those with clinical hepatitis should be retested upon hospital admission for delivery. Women at risk for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection should also be vaccinated. To avoid misinterpreting transient positive HBsAg results within 21 days of vaccination, HBsAg testing should be performed before vaccination. Laboratories conducting HBsAg tests should use FDA-cleared tests and follow the manufacturer’s labeling, including confirmatory testing of initially reactive specimens with a licensed neutralizing confirmatory test. When HBsAg testing is performed at delivery, shortened testing protocols may be used, and initially reactive results should prompt expedited administration of immunoprophylaxis to infants. 4. Chlamydia Testing: All pregnant women should be routinely tested for Chlamydia trachomatis at the first prenatal visit. Women under 25 years of age and those at increased risk for chlamydia (e.g., with new or multiple sexual partners) should be retested during the third trimester to prevent maternal postnatal complications and chlamydial infection in the infant. Screening during the first trimester may prevent adverse effects of chlamydia during pregnancy, but evidence supporting this is limited. If screening is performed only during the first trimester, there is a longer period for potential infection acquisition before delivery. 5. Gonorrhea Testing: Pregnant women at risk for gonorrhea or living in areas with high Neisseria gonorrhoeae prevalence should be tested at the first prenatal visit. A repeat test should be performed during the third trimester for those at continued risk. 6. Hepatitis C Testing: Pregnant women at high risk for hepatitis C infection should be tested for hepatitis C antibodies at the first prenatal visit.
